title: Ruby AI Tutor — Senior Phase Level 10 Question Bank

contexts.A: Persuasive / opinion text — argues a position on a topic.
contexts.B: Expository / information text — presents factual information without taking a side.
contexts.C: Paired or multi-source texts (synthesis/comparison tasks) — used together for integrated response.
contexts.D: Logical argument form — premises and conclusion presented for validity evaluation.

masteryRules.registerEnforcement: HARD — academic register required across all L10 written and oral tasks
masteryRules.ambitiousGrammarPolicy: Items with a complex grammar requirement (multi-paragraph essays) require grammar GREEN or AMBER overall, with no single error category above 20% (RED)

scoringBands.amberPolicy: AMBER alone does not fail progression — triggers targeted practice and is logged.
scoringBands.registerViolation: any contraction or slang in HARD register skills is flagged and must be replaced before acceptance

forbidden: contractions (don't, won't, can't, it's, I'm, they're, you're, etc.)
slang (kids, guys, stuff, awesome, cool, vibe, etc.)
informal first-person framing without academic alternative (I think, I feel, like, sort of)
exclamation marks for emphasis (! used to intensify rather than mark a genuine exclamation)
second-person address as default (you should, you might) — use the third person or formal first person
acceptedAlternatives: 'In my view, supported by the evidence, ___'
academicRegisterRules.scoring: Any forbidden item present in a response is flagged. Responses with ≥1 forbidden item in a HARD-register skill cannot achieve GREEN on register; ≥2 forbidden items move register to RED.

grammarRules.policy: For essay skills (C1, C3, C4), grammar must be GREEN or AMBER overall, and no single category may be RED.

texts.title: Why Social Media Helps Teens
texts.passage: Social media is one of the best things to happen to young people in the last twenty years. Imagine a shy 13-year-old in a small town who finds an online community of other young writers — suddenly the world is wider. Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute have published findings consistent with a 'Goldilocks' hypothesis: moderate use of social media is linked with similar or slightly higher life satisfaction than no use at all, while very heavy use is linked with lower satisfaction. The clearest gains come from staying in touch with friends and family who live far away. Should we really cut young people off from the very tools that help them find their tribe?

The clearest gains come from staying in touch with friends and family who live far away. Should we really cut young people off from the very tools that help them find their tribe?

texts.title: Why Social Media Harms Teens
texts.passage: Pause and consider what has changed in the last fifteen years that lines up with rising teenage anxiety: social media. Researchers including Dr Jean Twenge have argued that depression rates among US teens began climbing in the early 2010s as smartphones spread, and that the climb tracks heavy social-media use closely. Endless scrolling, comparison with filtered lives, and the pressure to perform are exhausting. Teenagers themselves — in survey after survey — say they feel worse after long sessions on the apps. We owe young people protection from a system designed to be addictive, not access to more of it.

texts.title: Act Fast on Climate
texts.passage: Time is running out, and the science could not be clearer. The IPCC's AR6 synthesis report (2023) confirmed that human activity has warmed the planet by about 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels and that limiting warming to 1.5°C requires deep, immediate cuts in greenhouse-gas emissions this decade. Every fraction of a degree matters: it is the difference between many coastal cities surviving and many coastal cities drowning. Doctors, scientists, and economists agree that bold action today costs less than disaster tomorrow. We owe our children a planet they can live on — and the time to act is now.

texts.title: Don't Rush Climate Policy
texts.passage: Yes, the climate is changing — but rushing into poorly designed policies can do more harm than good. When Germany accelerated its nuclear shutdown after Fukushima, the country burned more coal for several years and electricity prices rose sharply. Working families, not politicians, paid the price. A measured transition that protects jobs and keeps the lights on will deliver better long-term outcomes than headline-grabbing pledges with no plan. Acting wisely matters more than acting fast.

texts.title: AI Tutors Belong in Every Classroom
texts.passage: Picture a Year 9 student stuck on quadratic equations at 9 p.m., with no one around to help. An AI tutor patiently explains the same problem ten different ways, never tires, and never makes the student feel stupid. Published research from Stanford's Graduate School of Education has reported measurable test-score gains for well-designed tutoring interventions, with effect sizes varying widely by study. Teachers are not replaced — they are freed from repetitive explaining to do what they do best. The question is not whether AI tutors belong in schools, but how soon we can get them to every learner.

texts.title: Slow Down on AI in Schools
texts.passage: Ask any teacher: what students need most is not more screens. OECD PISA analyses have repeatedly raised concerns that heavy classroom use of technology is associated with weaker basic-skills outcomes when devices replace rather than supplement teaching. AI tutors may help with practice, but they cannot read a child's frustration the way a human can. They also make confident mistakes — and a confident, fluent error from an AI is far harder to spot than a wrong answer in a textbook. Pause, evaluate, and bring AI in only where it earns its place.

texts.title: Close City Centres to Cars
texts.passage: Pedestrian-only city centres make towns more pleasant for everyone. When Pontevedra in Spain closed its centre to cars in 1999, the share of children walking to school rose sharply, air pollution measurably improved, and small shops in the pedestrian zone reported steady or rising takings. Madrid, Oslo, and Ghent have since adopted similar measures and seen similar results. The simplest and cheapest way to make a city centre safer, cleaner, and more economically vibrant is also one of the oldest: give the streets back to the people who walk them.

texts.title: Don't Lock Out the People Who Need Cars
texts.passage: Closing a city centre to cars can sound progressive but make life harder for the people most likely to depend on a car: older shoppers who cannot walk long distances, parents with small children and heavy bags, disabled drivers with blue badges, and small-business owners whose vans deliver supplies. Without careful design — accessible pick-up points, generous exemptions, and good public transport — pedestrian-only zones risk excluding the people they should welcome most. The lesson from successful schemes is that detail and exemptions matter as much as the headline ban.

texts.title: Ban Single-Use Plastic
texts.passage: Single-use plastic is choking the planet. After Ireland introduced a small charge on plastic bags in 2002, use fell by over 90 percent within a year, and roadside litter dropped noticeably. Kenya, Rwanda, and Bangladesh have all introduced similar measures with similar success. The good news is clear: bans work when they are designed well and communicated honestly. A simple law can change behaviour overnight in ways that decades of voluntary recycling campaigns never managed.

texts.title: Bans Are Not the Whole Answer
texts.passage: Plastic bans solve part of the problem but create others. A widely-cited Danish life-cycle analysis suggested that a thick cotton tote must be reused many times — well over a hundred — to match the lifetime carbon footprint of a thin plastic bag. People who buy several cotton bags but rarely use them may do more environmental harm than good. Plastic also has real uses: it keeps food fresh and cuts waste in the supply chain. The smarter approach combines targeted bans with better recycling and consumer education, not a single sharp policy alone.

texts.title: Lower the Voting Age to 16
texts.passage: Lowering the voting age to 16 brings young people into democratic life at the moment they are forming their views. Scotland lowered the age for its 2014 independence referendum, and turnout among 16- and 17-year-old voters was reported by Scottish researchers to be very high — higher in fact than among voters aged 18 to 24. The data undermines the simple claim that 16-year-olds are too disengaged to participate. Given clear civic education and good information, the youngest voters in Scotland turned out to be among the most thoughtful.

texts.title: Keep the Voting Age at 18
texts.passage: Voting is a serious civic responsibility, and the threshold of 18 has been chosen carefully across most democracies. At 16, most young people are still in compulsory schooling and have not yet experienced the full responsibilities of work, tax, or independent housing that shape adult political choices. Lowering the age risks making participation a school exercise rather than an adult choice. A better path is stronger civic education before 18, so that when young people do vote, they vote informed and free.

texts.title: Free School Meals for All
texts.passage: Free school meals should be universal in every primary school. Children learn better when they are not hungry, and families on tight budgets benefit most. A 2017 UK government evaluation of universal free school meals found small but measurable improvements in academic performance for primary-school pupils, and savings for families. The cost to taxpayers is real but modest, and it returns to the economy through better learning, better attendance, and less administrative work checking eligibility.

The cost to taxpayers is real but modest, and it returns to the economy through better learning, better attendance, and less administrative work checking eligibility.

texts.title: Target the Children Who Need Help
texts.passage: Universal free meals sound generous but spread limited resources thinly. Many of the children who eat the meals would have eaten well at home; the public money would do more good directed at the families that need it most. A targeted system — clearly communicated and easy to apply for — can lift the same children out of food poverty at a fraction of the universal cost. Generosity is not the same as good design; care for poorer families means real focus, not headline universality.

texts.title: Make P.E. Mandatory Every Week
texts.passage: Two hours of compulsory school sport every week protects the lifelong health of every pupil. The Department of Health in England has long recommended at least one hour a day of moderate activity for children. School is the one place where every child can be reached, regardless of family resources or local facilities. A compulsory minimum guarantees access; an optional minimum guarantees that the children who most need movement are the most likely to opt out. The choice for policymakers is simple.

texts.title: Compulsory P.E. Misses the Point
texts.passage: Forcing every pupil into the same sports lessons does not make them love movement. Many of the people most reluctant to exercise as adults trace it to humiliating school P.E. lessons. A better model offers a wide menu — dance, walking, swimming, climbing, team sports — and lets pupils choose, with clear minimum hours. The goal is a lifelong habit, not a captive class. Quality and choice matter more than universal compulsion.

texts.title: The Case for Universal Basic Income
texts.passage: Universal basic income would give every adult a small regular payment, regardless of work or income. A multi-year Finnish pilot ending in 2018 reported improvements in wellbeing among recipients, even where the effect on employment was small. As automation reduces some kinds of work, a basic floor of income provides stability and choice. People can start businesses, return to education, or care for family members without falling into poverty. UBI may sound radical, but it is one of the simplest answers to a changing economy.

People can start businesses, return to education, or care for family members without falling into poverty. UBI may sound radical, but it is one of the simplest answers to a changing economy.

texts.title: Universal Basic Income Is the Wrong Tool
texts.passage: Basic income for every adult sounds generous but is wasteful. Most of the money goes to people who do not need it, and the same budget could lift far more poorer households out of hardship through targeted support, better housing, and skilled job training. Universal payments also risk eroding the link between effort and reward that has shaped successful economies for centuries. The pilots are encouraging on wellbeing but inconclusive on the wider economy. Better-targeted policy beats universal generosity.

texts.title: End Animal Testing
texts.passage: Modern science no longer needs animal testing for most cosmetic and many medical purposes. The European Union banned cosmetics testing on animals in 2013 and has seen no decline in product safety. Advances in organ-on-a-chip technology, computer modelling, and synthetic skin tests can already replace many animal experiments. Continuing to use animals when better methods exist is cruelty by habit, not by necessity. A clear timetable for phasing out remaining tests would push science forward.

Continuing to use animals when better methods exist is cruelty by habit, not by necessity. A clear timetable for phasing out remaining tests would push science forward.

texts.title: Animal Testing Still Has a Role
texts.passage: Despite real advances in alternatives, some medical research still depends on whole-system animal studies — testing how a new treatment affects a living body, not a chip in a lab. The vaccines, surgical techniques, and cancer treatments that save lives every day were almost all tested on animals before they reached patients. Tight regulation, ethical review, and the '3Rs' framework — replace, reduce, refine — already require researchers to minimise harm. Rushing to abolition risks slowing down treatments that save human lives.

texts.title: School Trips Are Essential
texts.passage: A field trip to a museum, a forest, or a city centre teaches in ways no classroom can match. A study from the University of Arkansas (Kisida and colleagues, 2014) from the University of Arkansas reported that pupils who visited an art museum showed measurable gains in critical thinking, empathy, and tolerance compared with peers who did not. Trips also build memories that bond a class together and connect lessons to the real world. Cutting trips to save money or time saves little and removes some of the most powerful learning experiences pupils have.

Trips also build memories that bond a class together and connect lessons to the real world. texts.title: Trips Cost More Than People Think
texts.passage: School trips look simple but add many hidden costs. Coaches, entry tickets, and lunches strain school budgets, and the cost is often passed on to families. Lower-income pupils may be quietly excluded even with help. Trips also lose lesson time, sometimes a whole day for a one-hour visit. The learning gains from a single trip do not always justify the disruption. Schools should focus on a few well-planned trips that genuinely link to the curriculum, rather than a long list of outings.

texts.title: Homework Builds Habits
texts.passage: Homework gives students important practice, and the habits it builds carry far beyond any single subject. Pupils who plan their time, gather their materials, and work without a teacher watching are learning skills they will use at university and at work. The amount must be sensible — the widely-cited rule of about ten minutes per grade level per night is a useful starting point — and the tasks must be well-designed. But the idea of homework, kept in reasonable proportion, has a real place in school.

But the idea of homework, kept in reasonable proportion, has a real place in school.

texts.title: Homework Does More Harm Than Good
texts.passage: Many young learners get more homework than they can usefully handle. After a full school day, children need rest, play, and family time more than another worksheet. Surveys of middle-school pupils repeatedly find high rates of stress around nightly homework, and stress reduces sleep, which reduces learning. Wealthier families can afford tutors and quiet study spaces, so homework often widens the gap between richer and poorer children. Schools should replace daily homework with short, optional projects pupils choose themselves.

texts.title: Ban Phones in Classrooms
texts.passage: Phones should be put away during lessons. Even on silent, a phone on a desk tempts the user to check it, and surveys consistently report short intervals between checks. Schools that have introduced lockable pouches at the door have reported steadier attention and small but measurable gains in classroom test scores. Phones also fuel anxiety: constant notifications keep many pupils in a low-level state of stress that makes deep work harder. A simple physical separation during lessons protects learning at very low cost.

texts.title: Phones Belong in Modern Classrooms
texts.passage: Banning phones in classrooms ignores how learning has changed. Pupils use phones to scan QR codes, translate words, record videos for projects, and check facts during discussions. Removing the device removes a useful tool. Teaching responsible use is more valuable than banning the device — when pupils practise putting their phones face down for set tasks and using them only when invited, they build self-control. Studies on outright bans show mixed results. Rather than a blanket ban, schools should design clear rules and trust learners to follow them.

texts.title: Eat Less Meat
texts.passage: Cutting back on meat is one of the most effective things ordinary people can do for the planet. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that livestock farming accounts for around 14.5 percent of human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions. Beef in particular is far more carbon-intensive per kilogram than plant foods. Around three-quarters of the world's farmland is used for animals, yet animals produce less than a fifth of the world's calories. Even cutting meat to two or three days a week shrinks a household's carbon footprint sharply.

Around three-quarters of the world's farmland is used for animals, yet animals produce less than a fifth of the world's calories. texts.title: Meat Still Has a Place
texts.passage: Ending meat-eating is not the simple answer it looks. In many regions, livestock graze on land that cannot grow crops, turning unusable grass into food. Pastoral farming also supports rural communities where few other industries exist. Meat is nutritionally dense — it provides iron, vitamin B12, and high-quality protein in forms the body absorbs easily. Plant-based diets can supply these nutrients but only with care, especially for young children and pregnant women. Responsible meat-eating — pasture-raised, less waste, smaller portions — is a better target than abolition.

texts.title: Remove Anonymous Accounts Online
texts.passage: Anonymous accounts make abuse easy. When people can post without consequences, they often say things they would never say to someone's face — and the targets are disproportionately women, minorities, and public figures. A verified-identity rule for major social-media platforms would not silence ordinary users; it would simply attach posts to real people, as a newspaper letter or a public meeting already does. The harms of anonymity online have grown faster than the benefits, and platforms should now act.

texts.title: Anonymity Protects the Vulnerable
texts.passage: For every troll an identity rule might silence, several whistle-blowers, abuse survivors, LGBTQ+ teenagers in unsafe homes, and dissidents under authoritarian governments would lose their only voice. Anonymous speech has a long and honourable history, from political pamphlets in the 18th century to civic exposes today. A rush to remove anonymity online risks harming the very people who most need protection. The smarter response is platform moderation that targets behaviour, not identity.

texts.title: Let Driverless Cars On the Roads
texts.passage: Driverless cars have been allowed on public roads in California, Arizona, and parts of Texas for several years now, and per-mile crash rates have been reported by operators as broadly comparable to or better than human drivers in similar settings, with the data dependent on operator-released figures, according to operator reports. Computers do not get tired, drunk, or distracted. Wider rollout, with careful regulation, could prevent tens of thousands of crashes a year. Cautious adoption now will deliver the next big public-health win on the roads.

texts.title: Slow Down on Driverless Cars
texts.passage: Driverless cars have been involved in high-profile crashes that human drivers might have avoided — and the data on average miles between serious incidents still depends heavily on which company you ask. Operators control their own safety data and have strong reasons to release flattering numbers. A genuinely independent regulator, with the power to audit, suspend, and punish, must come before mass rollout. Until that is in place, every new mile of driverless deployment is a public experiment without proper consent.

texts.title: Source 1: Aerobic Exercise & Memory (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, summary)
texts.passage: Reviews of aerobic-exercise research in older adults have consistently found that regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with reduced age-related hippocampal shrinkage and improved memory performance compared with sedentary controls. Effect sizes reported across studies are modest but broadly consistent.

texts.title: Source 2: Combined Aerobic + Strength Training (JAMA Network Open, summary)
texts.passage: Summaries of randomised trials in older adults suggest that combining aerobic exercise with strength training over many months tends to produce larger cognitive improvements than aerobic exercise alone. Many authors in this area recommend that exercise programmes for adults over 65 include both aerobic and strength components.

texts.title: Source 3: Intensity Risks (British Journal of Sports Medicine)

The recommended approach is a moderate, progressive one, with supervision in the early weeks.

texts.title: Source 1: Tallinn Free Transport
texts.passage: After Tallinn made public transport free for residents in 2013, the city reported a meaningful fall in car traffic in the centre within two years. The policy is widely cited in transport-policy debates as evidence that demand for public transport responds strongly to price.

texts.title: Source 2: Luxembourg National Free Transport
texts.passage: Luxembourg made public transport free nationally in 2020. Crowding rose only modestly on the busiest routes, and the government responded by adding capacity where needed. The Luxembourg case shows that universal free transport is operationally feasible at national scale.

texts.passage: The International Energy Agency has consistently noted that solar generation is intermittent and varies with daylight, weather, and season. skills.name: Distinguish fact, inference, and speculation
skills.description: Distinguish fact, inference, and speculation in a statement.
skills.defaultPrompt: Read the statement. Classify it as FACT (verifiable data), INFERENCE (likely conclusion from data — 'suggests', 'tends to', 'probably'), or SPECULATION (possibility about the future or unknown — 'might', 'may', 'could' + future). Give a one-sentence reason. Use academic register.
tolerance: signal-word identification accepted as justification
academic register required

recovery.action: Three-category sort drill with signal-word focus.
Highlight future-tense and 'might/may' signal words; learner re-classifies.
Sentence frame: 'This is [CATEGORY] because ___.'

skills.name: Compare argumentative strategies
skills.gate: ≥60% accuracy; comparison language present; 4 text pairs; 2 sessions
skills.description: Compare the argumentative strategies of two persuasive texts on the same topic. Uses 16 distinct text pairs covering varied topics (vs. only 6 in v1).
skills.questionFormat: ≥2 strategies per text + ≥1 similarity + ≥1 difference with comparison language
skills.defaultPrompt: Read both texts. Identify ≥2 argumentative strategies used in each. State ≥1 similarity and ≥1 difference. Use comparison language. Use academic register.
tolerance: strategy synonyms accepted (e.g. 'data' for 'statistics', 'expert testimony' for 'expert citation')
comparison language: both/while/whereas/in contrast/on the other hand/similarly
academic register required

recovery.action: Strategy catalogue + identification drill.
Evidence-first: highlight the strategy in the text before naming it.
Text-based strategy comparison frame required before free response.

skills.name: Identify and explain a counter-argument
skills.gate: ≥60% counter-argument identification accuracy; all 3 components present; 6 texts; 2 sessions
skills.description: Identify a counter-argument within a persuasive text, describe how the author responds, and evaluate the quality of that response.
skills.defaultPrompt: Read the persuasive text. (1) State the counter-argument the writer acknowledges. (2) Describe how the author addresses or responds to it. (3) Evaluate the quality of the author's response — is it convincing? Why? Use academic register.
tolerance: paraphrased counter-argument accepted
any reasoned evaluation accepted (convincing / partially / not convincing) with a stated reason
academic register required

recovery.action: Counter-argument signal-word focus: however / admittedly / while some argue / opponents might say / detractors / critics say.
Highlight the sentence after the counter-argument signal; learner re-reads.
Sentence frame: 'The author's response is/is not convincing because ___.'

items.passage: Every school should offer free breakfast to all pupils. Some argue that this is too expensive for taxpayers to fund. However, evaluations of universal infant free school meals in England in 2014–2017 reported attainment gains in primary-school pupils alongside savings on administration and breakfast-club running costs. The cost concern is real, but the evidence is that universal breakfasts return more than they cost.
items.prompt: (1) State the counter-argument the writer acknowledges. (2) Describe how the author responds to it. (3) Evaluate the quality of the author's response.
items.question: (1) State the counter-argument the writer acknowledges. (2) Describe how the author responds to it. (3) Evaluate the quality of the author's response.

checks.description: Identifies the counter-argument: the policy is too expensive for taxpayers to fund.
Describes the author's response: cites the 2014–2017 UK universal infant free school meals evaluation showing attainment gains and administrative savings.
Gives a reasoned evaluation (acceptable answer: convincing — the response cites a named real-world evaluation directly addressing cost). Any stance accepted if reasoning is sound.
Academic register — no contractions or slang.

skills.name: Three-source synthesis
skills.gate: All 4 checks ≥60% across 3 synthesis tasks; 3 sessions
skills.description: Synthesize information from three sources into a coherent integrated summary with citation language.
skills.questionFormat: integrated synthesis paragraph using all three sources with attribution
skills.defaultPrompt: Read the three sources. Write one integrated paragraph that uses ≥1 specific detail from each source, attributes each with citation language, and integrates them rather than describing each in turn. Use academic register.
tolerance: citation phrases: according to / as stated in / argues that / reports that / the study found / the authors note

recovery.action: Source map: one key point per source confirmed before writing.
Citation menu enforced: every sourced claim must use citation phrase.
Integration frame: one sentence referencing all three sources required before drafting.

Source 1 — Source 1: Aerobic Exercise & Memory (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, summary)
Reviews of aerobic-exercise research in older adults have consistently found that regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with reduced age-related hippocampal shrinkage and improved memory performance compared with sedentary controls. Effect sizes reported across studies are modest but broadly consistent.

Source 2 — Source 2: Combined Aerobic + Strength Training (JAMA Network Open, summary)
Summaries of randomised trials in older adults suggest that combining aerobic exercise with strength training over many months tends to produce larger cognitive improvements than aerobic exercise alone. Many authors in this area recommend that exercise programmes for adults over 65 include both aerobic and strength components.

Source 3 — Source 3: Intensity Risks (British Journal of Sports Medicine)
Reviews of exercise prescription for older adults have cautioned that high-intensity exercise programmes in adults over 70 are associated with raised risks of falls and joint injury when not properly supervised. The recommended approach is a moderate, progressive one, with supervision in the early weeks.

Source 1 — Source 1: Tallinn Free Transport
After Tallinn made public transport free for residents in 2013, the city reported a meaningful fall in car traffic in the centre within two years. The policy is widely cited in transport-policy debates as evidence that demand for public transport responds strongly to price.

Source 2 — Source 2: Luxembourg National Free Transport
Luxembourg made public transport free nationally in 2020. Crowding rose only modestly on the busiest routes, and the government responded by adding capacity where needed. The Luxembourg case shows that universal free transport is operationally feasible at national scale.

Source 3 — Source 3: Funding Trade-offs (LSE working paper)
Comparative analyses of free public-transport schemes argue that universal free transport delivers measurable equity gains at significant fiscal cost. Comparisons with targeted travel subsidies typically conclude that targeted subsidies deliver more equity per pound, while universal schemes are simpler to administer.

The International Renewable Energy Agency reports that the global cost of electricity from large solar farms fell dramatically between 2010 and 2022 — by roughly 89 percent according to IRENA's published figures. In many regions solar is now the cheapest source of new electricity generation.

Source 2 — Source 2: Intermittency (IEA)
The International Energy Agency has consistently noted that solar generation is intermittent and varies with daylight, weather, and season. Without sufficient storage and grid flexibility, very high solar shares can strain the electricity system. Source 3 — Source 3: Mineral Demands (USGS / IEA Critical Minerals)
Reports from the US Geological Survey and the IEA's Critical Minerals work note that scaling up solar requires sharply increased supply of materials including silver, copper, and silicon. Securing these supplies sustainably is now part of any serious clean-energy plan.

Source 1 — Source 1: Aerobic Exercise & Memory (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, summary)
Reviews of aerobic-exercise research in older adults have consistently found that regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with reduced age-related hippocampal shrinkage and improved memory performance compared with sedentary controls. Effect sizes reported across studies are modest but broadly consistent.

Source 2 — Source 2: Combined Aerobic + Strength Training (JAMA Network Open, summary)
Summaries of randomised trials in older adults suggest that combining aerobic exercise with strength training over many months tends to produce larger cognitive improvements than aerobic exercise alone. Many authors in this area recommend that exercise programmes for adults over 65 include both aerobic and strength components.

Source 3 — Source 3: Intensity Risks (British Journal of Sports Medicine)
Reviews of exercise prescription for older adults have cautioned that high-intensity exercise programmes in adults over 70 are associated with raised risks of falls and joint injury when not properly supervised. The recommended approach is a moderate, progressive one, with supervision in the early weeks.

Source 1 — Source 1: Tallinn Free Transport
After Tallinn made public transport free for residents in 2013, the city reported a meaningful fall in car traffic in the centre within two years. The policy is widely cited in transport-policy debates as evidence that demand for public transport responds strongly to price.

Source 2 — Source 2: Luxembourg National Free Transport
Luxembourg made public transport free nationally in 2020. Crowding rose only modestly on the busiest routes, and the government responded by adding capacity where needed. The Luxembourg case shows that universal free transport is operationally feasible at national scale.

Source 3 — Source 3: Funding Trade-offs (LSE working paper)
Comparative analyses of free public-transport schemes argue that universal free transport delivers measurable equity gains at significant fiscal cost. Comparisons with targeted travel subsidies typically conclude that targeted subsidies deliver more equity per pound, while universal schemes are simpler to administer.

Source 1 — Source 1: Solar Cost Falls (IRENA)
The International Renewable Energy Agency reports that the global cost of electricity from large solar farms fell dramatically between 2010 and 2022 — by roughly 89 percent according to IRENA's published figures. In many regions solar is now the cheapest source of new electricity generation.

Source 2 — Source 2: Intermittency (IEA)
The International Energy Agency has consistently noted that solar generation is intermittent and varies with daylight, weather, and season. Without sufficient storage and grid flexibility, very high solar shares can strain the electricity system. The IEA recommends combining solar with storage, demand management, and complementary low-carbon sources.

Source 3 — Source 3: Mineral Demands (USGS / IEA Critical Minerals)
Reports from the US Geological Survey and the IEA's Critical Minerals work note that scaling up solar requires sharply increased supply of materials including silver, copper, and silicon. Securing these supplies sustainably is now part of any serious clean-energy plan.

A World Health Organization review summarised research finding microplastic particles in many samples of bottled water. The health implications remain uncertain, but the WHO recommended further research and continued policy attention.

After Tallinn made public transport free for residents in 2013, the city reported a meaningful fall in car traffic in the centre within two years. The policy is widely cited in transport-policy debates as evidence that demand for public transport responds strongly to price.

Source 2 — Source 2: Luxembourg National Free Transport
Luxembourg made public transport free nationally in 2020. Crowding rose only modestly on the busiest routes, and the government responded by adding capacity where needed. The Luxembourg case shows that universal free transport is operationally feasible at national scale.

Source 3 — Source 3: Funding Trade-offs (LSE working paper)
Comparative analyses of free public-transport schemes argue that universal free transport delivers measurable equity gains at significant fiscal cost. Comparisons with targeted travel subsidies typically conclude that targeted subsidies deliver more equity per pound, while universal schemes are simpler to administer.

The International Renewable Energy Agency reports that the global cost of electricity from large solar farms fell dramatically between 2010 and 2022 — by roughly 89 percent according to IRENA's published figures. In many regions solar is now the cheapest source of new electricity generation.

Source 2 — Source 2: Intermittency (IEA)
The International Energy Agency has consistently noted that solar generation is intermittent and varies with daylight, weather, and season. Without sufficient storage and grid flexibility, very high solar shares can strain the electricity system. The IEA recommends combining solar with storage, demand management, and complementary low-carbon sources.

Source 3 — Source 3: Mineral Demands (USGS / IEA Critical Minerals)
Reports from the US Geological Survey and the IEA's Critical Minerals work note that scaling up solar requires sharply increased supply of materials including silver, copper, and silicon. Securing these supplies sustainably is now part of any serious clean-energy plan.

Reviews of aerobic-exercise research in older adults have consistently found that regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with reduced age-related hippocampal shrinkage and improved memory performance compared with sedentary controls. Effect sizes reported across studies are modest but broadly consistent.

Source 2 — Source 2: Combined Aerobic + Strength Training (JAMA Network Open, summary)
Summaries of randomised trials in older adults suggest that combining aerobic exercise with strength training over many months tends to produce larger cognitive improvements than aerobic exercise alone. Many authors in this area recommend that exercise programmes for adults over 65 include both aerobic and strength components.

Source 3 — Source 3: Intensity Risks (British Journal of Sports Medicine)
Reviews of exercise prescription for older adults have cautioned that high-intensity exercise programmes in adults over 70 are associated with raised risks of falls and joint injury when not properly supervised. The recommended approach is a moderate, progressive one, with supervision in the early weeks.

Studies in urban-forestry journals have estimated that mid-sized cities receive substantially larger returns from mature urban trees — through cooling, stormwater capture, and air-quality improvement — than they spend on tree care, when maintenance is planned for over the lifetime of the trees.

The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that a substantial share of the world's food crops depend on insect pollinators, with honeybees among the most important pollinator species. Many fruit and nut crops, including apples, almonds, and blueberries, produce little without bee visits.

Source 2 — Source 2: Pesticide Effects (EU EFSA)
The European Food Safety Authority has reviewed evidence on neonicotinoid pesticides and concluded that some uses present risks to bees. The EU has restricted several neonicotinoids on this basis. Some field studies after these restrictions have reported partial recovery of pollinator populations in particular regions.

Source 3 — Source 3: Wildflower Verges (Ecography)
Field studies of wildflower verges along farm roads have reported notably greater numbers of bee species than on mown grass verges in the same area. Researchers in this area recommend wildflower verges as a low-cost intervention for farm-scale pollinator support.

After Tallinn made public transport free for residents in 2013, the city reported a meaningful fall in car traffic in the centre within two years. The policy is widely cited in transport-policy debates as evidence that demand for public transport responds strongly to price.

Source 2 — Source 2: Luxembourg National Free Transport

Comparative analyses of free public-transport schemes argue that universal free transport delivers measurable equity gains at significant fiscal cost. Comparisons with targeted travel subsidies typically conclude that targeted subsidies deliver more equity per pound, while universal schemes are simpler to administer.

Source 1 — Source 1: Solar Cost Falls (IRENA)
The International Renewable Energy Agency reports that the global cost of electricity from large solar farms fell dramatically between 2010 and 2022 — by roughly 89 percent according to IRENA's published figures. In many regions solar is now the cheapest source of new electricity generation.

The International Energy Agency has consistently noted that solar generation is intermittent and varies with daylight, weather, and season. Without sufficient storage and grid flexibility, very high solar shares can strain the electricity system. The IEA recommends combining solar with storage, demand management, and complementary low-carbon sources.

Source 3 — Source 3: Mineral Demands (USGS / IEA Critical Minerals)
Reports from the US Geological Survey and the IEA's Critical Minerals work note that scaling up solar requires sharply increased supply of materials including silver, copper, and silicon. Securing these supplies sustainably is now part of any serious clean-energy plan.

checks.description: Introduction contains a single, clear thesis sentence matching one of the expected thesis patterns: 'This essay argues that X because Y' / 'While some argue X, the evidence suggests Y' / 'X is the stronger choice because A, B, and C'.
Thesis takes a defensible position on: Should the working week be reduced to 32 hours with no pay cut?. (either side acceptable)
Each body paragraph contains claim + ≥1 specific evidence reference (named source, study, dated case, or specific statistic) + explanation interpreting the evidence.

Evidence cited is drawn from grounded, specific sources (acceptable: 4 Day Week Foundation trial data; Iceland 2015-2019 trial; Microsoft Japan 2019 trial reports on productivity (claims have been debated)). Vague gestures and unsupported anecdotes (e.g. 'Less work is better'; one anecdote; appeal to wellbeing without productivity data) do not count.
≥2 transitions between paragraphs (However, Furthermore, In addition, Nevertheless, By contrast, Moreover, Consequently). Transition words must appear at the start of a sentence linking paragraphs.
Conclusion paraphrases the thesis and does not introduce new evidence.

Academic register throughout: no contractions, no slang, no informal first-person, no exclamation marks used for emphasis.

skills.name: Write a counter-argument and rebuttal paragraph

skills.description: Write one paragraph that acknowledges a counter-argument and responds with a rebuttal supported by evidence, while remaining consistent with the main claim.
skills.defaultPrompt: Write a single paragraph that defends the claim. Acknowledge a strong counter-argument with an explicit signal, respond with a rebuttal signal, and back the rebuttal with specific evidence. Stay consistent with the main claim. Use academic register.
tolerance: counter signals: 'Some argue', 'It might be said', 'Critics claim', 'Opponents say', 'One might object'
rebuttal signals: 'However', 'Yet', 'Nevertheless', 'On the contrary', 'In response', 'Despite this'
any reasonable evidence accepted if specific and named
academic register required

rebuttal signals: 'However', 'Yet', 'Nevertheless'
academic register required at HARD

All content is relevant to the topic: Should compulsory financial literacy be added to the curriculum?. No off-topic clauses.
